flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
Well, it's always like at the beginning of school, you know, kids have a very hard time adjusting to a new environment. And at first I ease it on, you know, I'll welcome everyone and then I'll get to know them. I'll tell the parents, hey, stay so we can get to know each other. And then one by one, I'll go up to the kid, introduce myself. And if it's like, oh, I saw one kid, she was really, really having a bad time. And I went over there, I got my bear from my classroom and I started talking in my bear voice. And she started looking around like, and I was like, oh, did I get you? Did I start it? She was like, no, no, no. And then I kept talking in that voice. She was like, thank you. And mom was like, oh, my God, you really got her. Like, you know, I was like, oh, you know, it's OK. And then she was like, do you mind if I, you know, video or call you back? And I was like, you know, it didn't bother me at all. But she was like, my kid grew to, you know. Love you. And she was just like, oh, my gosh. She was like, that's all she talks about. Miss Kendra just, when I'm not doing well, she talks to me like she's Elmo. And I was like, and the mom was like, did you know that she watched Elmo or something? Because you went right to Elmo. I said, well, usually Elmo gets the job done. Like, oh, my God, you know. And she was like, oh, my gosh. She was like, I was like, she said, I asked my husband, did we write it on the paper that she likes Elmo or something? And he was like, no, they didn't ask that. And so I was like, oh, okay. So.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you felt overwhelmed at work with children present. What did you do to manage yourself?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q4 Attempt 1]
Well, the kids don't really get me stressed. It's usually the adults that we work with. But, yeah, I don't, truthfully, I don't lose it in front of children. I go into their era, and then I'll just tell the teacher, like, can we talk about this later? Like, we'll talk once the children are done or, you know. And then I just gather myself, and then I think about, you know, everybody goes through things in life. So it could have been, you know, then when we started off, I said, oh, okay, well, what happened? Like, why did you come in storming and upset? And then the teacher was like, I thought you took something. And she was like, but I apologize. She said, I noticed when you looked and was like, can we talk a little bit later? That, you know, she said, I realized, oh, you really didn't take whatever it was that I needed or something. And she said, and I was like, oh, okay. And she was like, I just, I'm just not, adults don't, I'm there for the children. So adults are more like, okay, I can just deal with you later type deal. Like, we can talk about this later because I'm not a person to anger fast. So truthfully, I knit, well, not knit. I make blankets, and I play games. So my, on my tablet. So in the moment, I just take a breather and then I play a game with the children.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or saying no. Walk me through exactly what you would do, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
Okay, so if I'm doing pamper changing, I'll say, oh, friend, it's time for a pamper changing. Let's go ahead, and I'm going to walk you here, or you can walk with yourself, whichever one you'd like. Ms. Kendra will walk with you, and I'm going to tell you what it is that we're going to do. We're going to come up here. I'm going to lay down the mat for you so that we can potty, so we can, you know, take your pamper off. And then I'm going to say, would you like to sit on the toilet to get you some time so we can do a little potty training? And then I have a song that I sing. Pee-pee in the potty, pee-pee in the potty, pee-pee in the potty, so can you. And then they'll cheer, I'll cheer, and I'll say, okay, great job. And then I'll give them a tissue and say, okay, you're going to wipe yourself, front them back to front, put it in the toilet, have them say, can you flush the toilet for me? And then I'll say, okay, since you're in a pull-up. Would you like to put it on? And I'll hand it to them. This is the front of your pull-up. This is the back. And I'll explain to them, it's just like underwear, but it's not little kiddie underwear until we outgrow this and we can wear our regular underwear. And then I'll say, okay, you'll put your right foot in. Then you'll put your left foot in. Then you'll take both hands and pull on the side, and you'll pull them up until they're nice and snug for you. And then I'll say, if they say, oh, I can't do it. I say, well, can I help you? I always make sure I ask them if I can help. So if I get the yes, you can help, or no, you can't help. If it's yes, I can help, I'll take one side, and I'll have them take one side, and I'll say, okay, we're going to pull on three. One, two, three. Then we'll pull it up. Usually, I don't take their pants all the way down, so it'll be right there at the bottom of their shoes. And then I'll tell them, okay, now we're going to pull up our pants. Then a button, if I have to, but usually in preschool, we don't have to button. Parents are really good with just drawstring. Afterwards. We're done with that. I'll say, well, let's place the pamper in the trash. We'll place the pamper in the trash, and I'll say, okay, now we're going to wash our hands. And then, can you help me sing along with the birthday song? And then we'll go, happy birthday. We'll sing that three times. Wash our hands. I'll say, well, let's wet our hands first. And then I'll say, let's grab for soap. And then sometimes if the soap dispenser doesn't work, I say, oh, they're playing a game with us. Let's go back under, get some more. Rub-a-dub-dub. Thanks for the rub. Then they'll go back in. We'll wash again. Then I'll tell them, I'll turn the water off because it's kind of dirty to do that. And I'll turn the water off. And then I'll say, it's my turn. Wash really quickly. And then I'll say, thanks for joining me. And then we'll go back out and have a seat. So I'll talk to them. We'll sit for a while. I'll get a book. I'll ask them if they'd like to read a book. And I usually have a potty training book. And then I'll let them warm up. And I say, well, when you're ready, come let me know that you're ready. And then we can go and begin. I want you to wash your hands because I said I don't want you to wash, you know, I don't want you to get potty trained or I don't want to bother with you.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Can you share something you’ve learned about children or yourself over time that changed how you approach your work?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q9 Attempt 1]
that everything takes time. Everybody feels something and everybody has a bad day. At first, I didn't believe that children should have bad days, but they do, you know, and it, we don't know what goes on in their household after five o'clock or whichever time it is that they're picked up to the morning. And when I first started off, I didn't, that wasn't, that wasn't on my mind. It was like, oh my God, like, what's going on? Like, what did you do, mom? You know? And I had to say, you know what? They're little adults and this is not, you know, at first I was like, well, hey, hey, you know what? It's okay. Your mom's going to bring, you have to come to school. And then it was like, no, well, you know, talk to your mom. And I tell all my parents too, make sure you let them know you're going to go to school tomorrow. This is still school. You know, I try to encourage and just talk. You know, I just make a, I've learned to communicate very well because like I tell the parents, this is your home too. You're not, and you're going to feel that your child is not having a good day at school. Even if I tell you, oh, they had a good day. So I try to make that first impression a lasting one.
